### page_1
Precambrian Research 107 (2001) 265–281
Magnetic fabrics and paleomagnetism of the
Storsjo¨n–Edsbyn deformation zone, central Sweden
Ha˚kan J. Mattsson *, Sten-A,ke Elming
Di6ision of Applied Geophysics , Lulea˚U n i6ersity of Technology , SE-97187 Lulea˚, Sweden
Accepted 13 October 2000
Abstract
A regional deformation zone, separating tectonomagmatic blocks in the central part of the Fennoscandian Shield,
has been studied using anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility and paleomagnetism in order to deﬁne the tectonic
character and age of the zone and to put the deformation into a plate tectonic context. The deformation zone (the
Storsjo¨n–Edsbyn Deformation Zone; SEDZ) separates the Ra ¨tan granite of the Trans Scandinavian Igneous Belt
(TIB) and the southern Svecofennian subprovince in the southwest from older Svecofennian granitoids of the central
Svecofennian subprovince in the northeast. The SEDZ is the most prominent deformation zone in a regional pattern
of NW–SE trending shear zones. On basis of AMS data the width of the zone, which cuts through 1.7–1.9 Ga old
rocks, is estimated at 10–12 km in its central–southern part and 20–25 km in its northern part. The orientations of
the susceptibility axes vary systematically across the zone, in a way that suggests that the SEDZ is a pure shear
dominated transpression zone caused by a compressive stress from the present SSW. Paleomagnetic data from a
dolerite sill (Plat 10°, Plon166°) and from a dyke (Plat 25°, Plon190°) that cut the SEDZ indicate that no
plastic deformation has occurred along the zone during the past 1.25 Ga, and probably not for the past 1.5–1.6 Ga.
AMS data do not point to any deformation of the 1.70 Ga old Ra ¨tan granite, which further limits the time span of
deformation. The main phase of deformation most likely took place between 1.80 and 1.70 Ga ago. The geological
evolution of this part of the Fennoscandian Shield at the time between 1.80 and 1.70 Ga ago is very complex and in
part still enigmatic. This time period involves magmatism of the TIB, which is related to eastward subduction. It also
comprises the beginning of the Gothian orogeny and the development of a regional system of transpressive
deformation zones. The compressive stress ﬁeld from the present SSW indicated in this study is interpreted to be
related to an initial stage of plate collision between the southwestern Scandinavian subprovince and older parts of the
Fennoscandian Shield. This collision resulted in a system of regional NW–SE trending intra-plate deformation zones,
one of which is the SEDZ © 2001 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.
Keywords: Magnetic anisotropy of susceptibility; Paleomagnetism; Proterozoic deformation zone; Sweden; Transpression

1. Introduction
The Fennoscandian Shield can be divided into a
number of tectonomagmatic blocks (Gaa ´l and

Gorbatschev, 1987; Elming et al., 1993), that are
separated by more or less well deﬁned tectonic
zones (Fig. 1). The tectonic blocks reﬂect a
geochronological zonation of the shield and a
better knowledge of the character of the deforma-
tion zones that separate them is vital for an
understanding of the geological evolution of
Fennoscandia.
The Svecofennian Domain of Paleoproterozoic
rocks dominates the central part of the Baltic
Shield. Along the western margin of the Svecofen-
nian domain an almost N–S trending area of
granitoid rocks, the Transscandinavian Igneous
Belt (TIB), was formed between 1.81 and 1.66
Ga ago (A,ha¨ll and Larson, 2000). The Storsjo¨n–
Edsbyn deformation zone (SEDZ) is a regional
tectonic zone that separates the TIB and the
southern Svecofennian subprovince from the cen-
tral Svecofennian subprovince (Fig. 1). The zone
trends in a NNW direction and extends for a

### page_3
H.J. Mattsson, S.A,. Elming : Precambrian Research 107 (2001) 265–281 267
distance of 200 km, and it forms the most
prominent part of a regional system of NW–SE
trending deformation zones in the central part of
the Baltic Shield (Bergman and Sjo ¨stro¨m, 1994)
(Fig. 1). These zones are believed to have devel-
oped during the time period 1.65–1.82 Ga ago
(Bergman and Sjo ¨stro¨m, 1994; Ho ¨gdahl et al.,
1996; Ho¨gdahl and Sjo¨stro¨m, 1999).
The beginning of the Gothian orogeny ( 
1.75–1.55 Ga; A ,ha¨ll and Larson, 2000) coincide
in time with the magmatism of the TIB. The
geological evolution of the TIB is fairly well docu-
mented (e.g. Ahl et al., 1999; A ,ha¨ll and Larson,
2000) whereas the origin and mechanisms of the
Gothian evolution are rather poorly understood
(A,ha¨ll and Larson, 2000). With this study we
want to contribute to a better understanding of
the tectonic evolution related to the Gothian
orogeny, and this we do by investigating the
SEDZ. Some questions to be answered are; what
is the type of deformation? Can we deﬁne the
paleo stress ﬁeld? Can we estimate the age of
deformation? Is it possible to put the development
of the SEDZ into a plate tectonic context? To
answer these questions we have used anisotropy
of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) and paleomag-
netism in a study concentrated in the northern
part of the zone, where it marks the boundary
between the Ra¨tan granite of the TIB in the west
and the Ljusdal batholith and Revsund granite of
the central Svecofennian subprovince in the east
(Fig. 1). A previously presented tectonic model of
the zone (Bergman and Sjo ¨stro¨m, 1994) is also
tested.
2. Geological setting
Three generations of granite–granodiorite mas-
sifs dominate the geology of the region (Fig. 1). In
the southeast there is the strongly foliated Ljusdal
batholith, a granodiorite that is 1.84 Ga old
(U–Pb, Delin, 1993). The Svecofennian orogeny,
with two phases of folding plus a partial migma-
tization (Lundqvist et al., 1990), re-worked the
batholith and gave rise to a regional schistosity
with mainly shallow dipping planes of foliation.
In the west there is the magnetite and hematite
bearing 1.70 Ga old Ra¨tan granite (U–Pb, Delin,
1996) that is related to the Transscandinavian
Igneous Belt (TIB). The rectangular shape of the
granite can be fairly well deﬁned from aeromag-
netic data and its eastern boundary coincides with
the SEDZ for 100 km. The grayish and
coarsely porphyritic 1.80 Ga old Revsund
granitoid batholith (U–Pb, Claesson and
Lundqvist, 1995) is emplaced in the northeast and
two minor intrusions of Revsund type granites
(1.80 Ga old, U–Pb; Delin, 1996) are emplaced
southwest of the SEDZ. In contrast with the
Ljusdal batholith, the Ra¨tan and Revsund grani-
toids have not undergone regional metamorphism
(Delin and Aaro, 1992; Lundqvist et al., 1990).
Dolerite sills and dykes intrude large areas of the
Ra¨tan and Revsund granitoids in the northern
part of the study area. They are thought to belong
to a major formation of dolerites that is found in
the central and northern parts of Sweden and also
in the south western parts of Finland. Radiomet-
ric dating (U–Pb) in the archipelago between
Sweden and Finland gives an age of 1.27 Ga of
these rocks (Suominen, 1991).
3. The Storsjo¨n–Edsbyn deformation zone
(SEDZ)
The system of NW–SE trending shear zones, to
which the SEDZ belongs, characterizes the struc-
tural evolution of the Svecofennian Domain (Fig.
1). Bergman and Sjo¨stro¨m (1994) distinguish four
groups of shear zones in the area of the SEDZ, (I)
plastic, syn metamorphic, (II) mostly plastic, ret-
rograde, (III) brittle-plastic and (IV) brittle, post-
metamorphic. Types (II) and (III) are believed to
be typical for the SEDZ whereas type (I) is con-
nected to the regional folding and thought to be
older. Type (IV) is the youngest in this classiﬁca-
tion (Bergman and Sjo ¨stro¨m, 1994). The age of
the type (II) and (III) shear zones is by Bergman
and Sjo¨stro¨m (1994) believed to be 1.6–1.7 Ga,
or possibly younger. However, U–Pb dating of
syn tectonic titanites in SEDZ-mylonites (area B;
Fig. 2) indicates an age of the deformation of
1.80 Ga (Ho¨gdahl et al., 1996). A number of
shear zones situated east and southeast of the

### page_4
H.J. Mattsson, S.A,. Elming : Precambrian Research 107 (2001) 265–281268
Fig. 2. Generalized geological map showing the study area in
central Sweden. The map is based on aeromagnetic data
(Geological Survey of Sweden) and simpliﬁed from Lun-
dega˚rdh et al. (1984), Lundqvist et al. (1990), Delin and Aaro
(1992, 1994).
the strain ellipsoid (Bergman and Sjo¨stro¨m, 1994).
The plastic mylonites (type II) in the northern
part of the SEDZ (area B in Fig. 2) show dip slip
lineation, whereas the brittle plastic shear zones
(type III) have sub-horizontal slip lineation, which
indicates a strike slip motion. Most of the shear
zones have sub-horizontal, NE–SW striking folia-
tion poles. Bergman and Sjo ¨stro¨m (1994) con-
clude that the SEDZ is a transpression zone with
a dextral strike slip component of c. 16km.
Bergman and Sjo¨stro¨m (1994) also suggest that
there is a causal relationship between the intru-
sion of the Ra¨tan granite and the SEDZ since the
magma would provide the necessary heat for the
deformation and the zone broadly follows the
eastern boundary of the granite. The zone how-
ever continuous 50 km south of the southern
boundary of the Ra ¨tan granite, which indicates
that the granitoid hardly is solely responsible for
the development of the SEDZ.
4. Methods and sampling sites
Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS)
was used to measure the petrofabric of rocks (e.g.,
Hrouda, 1982). Basically, the AMS of a rock is
described by a second-order tensor. This tensor
can be visualized by an ellipsoid having three
principal axes of maximum, intermediate and
minimum susceptibility ( k
max, kint and kmin, re-
spectively). For multi-domain magnetite the kmax
axis is parallel to the long axis of an ellipsoidal
grain and for most rocks the kmax corresponds to
the mineral lineation, whereas the kmin axis corre-
sponds to the pole to the plane of foliation (Tar-
ling and Hrouda, 1993). The degree of anisotropy
is characterized by Pk
max:kmin and the shape of
the anisotropy ellipsoid is deﬁned by the shape
parameter T (Jelı´nek, 1981). If 1BTB0t h e
ellipsoid is prolate (cigar-shaped) and if 0 BTB1
the ellipsoid is oblate (disc-shaped); if T0t h e
ellipsoid is neutral. The AMS and temperature
variation of magnetic susceptibility of rocks were
measured with a Kappabridge KLY-3 and a CS-3
apparatus, respectively (Geofyzika Brno). The
statistical analysis of the AMS data was per-
formed using the technique of Jelı ´nek (1978).
SEDZ, suggested being related to a pattern of
NW–SE trending zones, are dated at 1.80–
1.82 Ga (U–Pb, Ho ¨gdahl and Sjo¨stro¨m, 1999).
A strain analysis indicates a non-coaxial defor-
mation of ﬂattening type with sub vertical maxi-
mum strain and a NW–SE striking XY plane of

### page_5
H.J. Mattsson, S.A,. Elming : Precambrian Research 107 (2001) 265–281 269
Direction and intensity of the remanent magne-
tization was measured with a spinner magnetome-
ter JR-5 (Geofyzika Brno) and a DC-SQUID
magnetometer (2G-Enterprises). Alternating ﬁeld
demagnetization was performed with coils incor-
porated in the DC-SQUID system and thermal
demagnetization was performed using a Schonst-
edt demagnetizer TSD-1. Remanent magnetiza-
tion directions were analyzed using Principle
Component Analysis (Kirschvink, 1980) and
means were calculated using the statistics of
Fisher (1953).
The samples were collected with a portable ﬁeld
drill and orientated with a magnetic and a sun
compass. In area A (Fig. 2) 135 drill cores were
collected at 16 sites distributed along a 33 km
long trajectory (Fig. 3). Twelve of these sites are
from the Ljusdal batholith (KA01–KA12) and
four are from the Revsund type granite (KA13–
KA16). In the northern part of area B (Fig. 2) 234
samples were collected at 20 sites. Seven sites are
situated in the Revsund granite (ST01–ST07), ﬁve
are from the Ra¨tan granite (ST11–ST15) and ﬁve
are dolerites (ST16–ST18, ST21–ST22) (Fig. 4).

The remaining sites are from two mylonites
(ST08–ST09) and one augen gneiss granite
(ST10). In the southern part of area B 89 drill
cores were collected at eight different localities,
including ﬁve dolerites (ST19–ST20, ST22, ST24,
ST26), one granite site (ST25) and two gneiss
rocks (ST27–ST28).
5. Results
5.1. Petrography
The rock in the four sites KA01–KA04 of the
Ljusdal batholith (Fig. 3) is a medium- to ﬁne-
grained granodiorite that possesses a sub-horizon-

### page_7
H.J. Mattsson, S.A,. Elming : Precambrian Research 107 (2001) 265–281 271
tal biotite foliation. It carries crystals of horn-
blende, biotite, plagioclase and quartz, without
signs of high-grade deformation. Apatite grains are
often associated with biotite. Magnetite and il-
menite lamellae dominate the opaque mineral frac-
tion.
In the central part of the SEDZ (sites KA05–
KA12, Fig. 3) the granodiorite has suffered from
variable degrees of chlorite alteration. Zones of
high-grade deformation are indicated by steeply
dipping foliation deﬁned by biotite and elongated
quartz grains.
The Revsund type granite west of the SEDZ
(sites KA13–KA16, Fig. 3) carries lamellae of
ilmenite that are frequently seen in between ﬂakes
of biotite. Magnetite crystals appear unaltered, and
they often surround the grains of ilmenite. A few
pyrite grains have borders of hematite, or iron
oxyhydroxide, which may indicate chemical
alteration.
The Revsund granite in the northeast (Fig. 1) is
coarse-grained and dominated by megacrysts of
plagioclase, microcline, quartz and biotite. The
three easternmost localities (ST01–ST03, Fig. 4)
are unaltered, apart from a minor chlorite alter-
ation of the rock at site ST01. West of these
localities, at sites ST04–ST07, the granite has a
steeply dipping biotite foliation trending NNW–
SSE. Gneisses, acid volcanics and banded plastic
mylonites (sites ST08–ST10, ST1 and ST21) deﬁne
the central part of the SEDZ with distinctly devel-
oped foliations that trend NW–SE and dip sub-ver-
tically. The microscope analysis of a sample from
site ST10 (augen gneiss granite) shows that some
magnetite grains are deformed and have an over-
growth of epidote, while others are cubic in shape
and appear unaltered. This indicates two genera-
tions of magnetite, of which the unaltered fraction
most likely is post-deformational.
The Ra¨tan granite (sites ST11–ST15) only shows
signs of low-grade deformation indicated by altered
mica crystals and fractures ﬁlled with ﬁne-grained
quartz and feldspars.
5.2. AMS
The aeromagnetic anomaly pattern of the Ljus-
dal batholith shows E–W trending anomalies in the
east that rotate clockwise to a NNW–SSE direction
when approaching the SEDZ. The rotation sug-
gests a dextral shear sense of the zone. The AMS
data of the batholith, east of the SEDZ (sites
KA01–KA04, area A), show sub-horizontal planes
of magnetic foliation and E–W striking magnetic
lineation (Fig. 3). The degree of anisotropy (P)
ranges from almost isotropic to more than 100%
anisotropy and most samples have oblate shaped
AMS ellipsoids (Fig. 3). Inside the deformation
zone (sites KA05–KA12) most planes of magnetic
foliation trend in a NNW–SSE direction and dip
sub-vertically. Maximum and intermediate suscep-
tibility axes are scattered or deﬁne a girdle pattern
(Fig. 5A), which results in prolate as well as oblate
shaped anisotropy ellipsoids. In the aeromagnetic
data this fabric is cut by a number of N–S trending
low magnetic lineaments. The sites at these linea-
ments, or close to them, have clustered anisotropy
axes with a sub-vertical lineation (Fig. 5B) and
mainly prolate ellipsoids. Rock magnetic data indi-
cate that magnetite is the main magnetic carrier in
the Ljusdal batholith both inside and outside of the
SEDZ (6A, 7B). However, some minor amounts of
hematite also contribute to the susceptibility (site
KA09), and at one site (KA03) the fabric is
completely governed by paramagnetic minerals
(Fig. 6A). The bulk susceptibility is similar between
the sites KA01–KA04 (outside the SEDZ) and the
sites KA05–KA12 (inside the SEDZ) (Fig. 7B).
The AMS data of the Revsund type granite
situated west of the SEDZ (sites KA13–KA16) do
not indicate a coherent fabric. However, most
samples have oblate shaped anisotropy ellipsoids
(Fig. 3). The poles to the magnetic foliation form
two clusters, one that trends SSW with a moderate
dip, and the other that is sub-horizontal and trends
ESE–WNW (Fig. 3). The magnetic lineations clus-
ter around a strike direction to the north with a
moderate dip. At site KA16 we can deﬁne a
preferred direction of the feldspars that trends
NW–SE, which is parallel to the magnetic foliation
plane.
In area B (Fig. 2) the magnetic fabric of the
Revsund granite at the localities ST01–ST03 is
rather poorly developed. The minimum principal
susceptibility axes deﬁne sub-vertical planes trend-

### page_8
H.J. Mattsson, S.A,. Elming : Precambrian Research 107 (2001) 265–281272
ing in various directions and the lineation varies
from sub-horizontal to sub-vertical. Closer to
the SEDZ, at the sites ST04–ST07, the magnetic
foliation has a NNW–SSE trending direction
and a sub-vertical dip, which is parallel to the
biotite foliation observed in the ﬁeld (Fig. 4).
The lineation mainly strikes SSE and dips mod-
erately, indicating a dominant strike-slip compo-
nent of deformation. Paramagnetic minerals
(most likely the observed biotite) is the main
carrier of magnetic susceptibility of the Revsund
granite, except at site ST05, which is a recrystal-
lized mylonite that carries magnetite (6B, 7A).
The degree of anisotropy is below 10% at the
unaltered sites (ST01–ST03) and only slightly
higher at the deformed sites (ST04–ST07).
In the mylonites and the gneissic rocks in the
center of the zone (sites ST08–ST10, ST16 and
ST21, Fig. 4) the poles to the magnetic foliation
are tightly clustered in the NE–SW direction,
with a sub-horizontal dip and the lineation clus-
ters sub-vertically. The fabric most likely ex-
presses a dominant NE–SW directed pure shear
component that results in a sub-vertical maxi-
mum ﬁnite strain.
The degree of anisotropy in specimens varies
from isotropic (site ST16) to P2.06 at site
ST09, which most likely reﬂects differences in
magnetic mineralogy; the mean susceptibility
K
mean0.0005790.00005 SI (site ST16),
Kmean0.00490.008 SI (site ST09). A linear re-
lation between P and Kmean, deﬁned at site
ST10, supports this (Fig. 6D).
Crossing the SEDZ westward and moving
into the Ra ¨tan granite, the magnetic foliation
planes of the rock at the sites ST11–ST12 are
parallel to the general direction of the zone
(Fig. 4). This orientation is also parallel to the
eastern boundary of the Ra ¨tan granite. Further
to the SW, at the sites ST13–ST15, the mag-
netic foliation has ﬂipped 90° to a sub-hori-
zontal orientation. The specimens are more
oblate shaped and the degree of anisotropy is
slightly higher at the sites ST11–ST12 than at
ST13–ST15 (Fig. 4). This points to a difference
in the stress conditions and a better grain align-
ment close to the contact than in the center of
the granitoid. There is also a difference in bulk
susceptibility between the sites at the boundary
[(ST11–ST12) Kmean 0.01590.008SI] and in
the center [(ST13–ST15) Kmean 0.0299
0.011SI], which indicates a possible enrichment
of iron oxides toward the center of the pluton.
The magnetic lineations of all the ﬁve sites
in the Ra ¨tan granite (ST11–ST15) are

sub-horizontal and strike NW–SE. This indicates
that a large area of the northeastern part of the
granite body has a sub-horizontal maximum ﬁnite
strain striking NW–SE. Rockmagnetic data show
that magnetite is the main carrier of the suscepti-
bility in the Ra¨tan granite (6C, 7C).
In the center of the SEDZ a dolerite sill trun-
cates the deformation pattern of a plastic my-
lonite rock (site ST16, Fig. 4). The average degree
of anisotropy of the sill is low ( P1.07) and
nothing indicates that the rock is deformed. Simi-
lar dolerite sills were sampled at four other locali-
ties outside the SEDZ (sites ST17–ST29) and
close to its center (site ST20). The magnetic fabric
of all ﬁve sites is consistent and they have sub-ver-
tical minimum anisotropy axes and maximum and
intermediate axes that deﬁne a girdle pattern in
the plane of foliation (Fig. 9B). This fabric is
considered characteristic for unaltered dolerite
sills (Knight and Walker, 1988). A 20 m wide
dolerite dyke at site 23 (Fig. 4) also seems to carry
a primary magnetic fabric, even though an inter-
pretation of aeromagnetic data indicates that the
dyke is cut by a NNW–SSE trending brittle shear
zone and dextrally displaced 400 m. The aver-
age degree of anisotropy is low ( P1.03) and the
principal axes of the AMS ellipsoid correlate well
with the dyke plane and its pole (Fig. 10B).
5.3. Paleomagnetism
Alternating ﬁeld demagnetization of samples
from the Ljusdal batholith (site KA02, Fig. 8A,B)
shows that the rocks east of the shear zone area
carry a stable remanent magnetization of decl. 
7° and incl. 25° ( a
9510°, k17; Table 1).
However, there is often an overlap in the coerciv-
ity spectra, which makes it difﬁcult to isolate the
characteristic magnetization. A great circle analy-
sis (Bailey and Halls, 1984) shows that the inter-
sections of the great circles (decl. 358°,
incl.30° and MAD12°; Fig. 8A) do not differ
signiﬁcantly from the mean direction deﬁned from
the vector diagrams (Table 1). This suggests that
we have been able to isolate an ancient magnetiza-
tion. The thermal data shows a wide range of
unblocking temperatures (Fig. 8C) and the ther-
mal mean direction is poorly constrained but it

The dolerite sill that truncates the plastic de-
formation pattern in the zone at site ST16 car-
ries a stable mean remanence direction after AF
demagnetization (decl. 29°, incl.  26°,
a
956° and k43) that is likely to represent
the primary magnetization of the rock (Table 1).
Together with the other dolerite sills (ST17–
ST20) a formation mean direction of decl. 32°
and incl.  23° (a
9510°, k56, 61 samples)
is deﬁned (Fig. 9A) and the calculated mean
paleopole position (Plat 12°, Plon162°, d
p
6° and dm11°) falls close to the 1.25 Ga refer-
ence pole on the APWP for the Fennoscandian
Shield (Fig. 11). This indicates that the sills are
of Postjotnian age. Thermal demagnetization
and other rock magnetic data shows that mag-
netite is the main carrier of both the remanence
and the susceptibility (Fig. 9C–E). The average
median destructive ﬁeld of 49 samples is 17 mT,
and together with the fairly high Q-values (Fig.
9F) it indicates that grains of pseudo-single do-
main size carry the remanence (Dunlop and
O8zdemir, 1997).
The NNE trending dolerite dyke at site ST23
(Fig. 4) carries a stable remanence in high alter-
nating ﬁelds and at high temperatures (Fig.
10C,D). A mean direction (decl. 5°, incl.
4°, a
958° and k26; Table 1) is deﬁned from
the thermal data (Fig. 10A) and the paleopole
(Plat25°, Plon 190°, d
p4° and dm8°)
calculated from this mean direction corresponds
to two possible paleomagnetic age intervals of
1.30–1.32 and 1.5–1.6 Ga (Fig. 11). Nei-
ther of these two time intervals are represented
in radiometric or paleomagnetic data from our
study area. However, 1.5–1.6 Ga old northeast
trending dykes with paleomagnetic directions
similar to that deﬁned at site ST23 have been
identiﬁed in a dyke swarm in the central Sve-
cofennian subprovince, 100 km north of the
SEDZ (Moakhar and Elming, 1998). It is possi-
ble that the dyke at site ST23 is related to this
dyke swarm, and therefore should be placed in
the 1.5–1.6 Ga time interval. The host rock of
the dyke has a foliation that is parallel to the
SEDZ, which, together with the close position
of the sampling site relative to the center of the
zone, indicates that the dyke post-dates all plas-
tic deformation activity of the zone in this area.

6. Discussion and conclusions
6.1. The character of the SEDZ
In the Ljusdal batholith a shear zone that cross-
cuts the rock close to the locality KA06 (Fig. 3)
deﬁnes the eastern boundary of the southern part
of the Storsjo¨n–Edsbyn deformation zone. East
of site KA06 the rock has magnetic foliation
planes with shallow dip towards the southeast and
sub-horizontal lineations that strike E–W. This
fabric is thought to represent a regional schistos-
ity. To the west of this site (at sites KA05–KA12)
the magnetic foliation planes dip steeply and show
mainly N–S or NNW–SSE trending strike direc-
tions. Since there is no geological or AMS evi-
dence that the Revsund type granite that was
sampled west of the zone (sites KA13–KA16) has
been subject to deformation caused by the SEDZ,
the width of the zone in this area can be estimated
to be 10–12 km.
Within the part of the Ljusdal batholith de-
formed by the SEDZ (sites KA05–KA12) two
AMS patterns are found. NNW–SSE trending
planes of magnetic foliation with maximum and
intermediate anisotropy axes that create a girdle
pattern deﬁne one type of fabric. This fabric has
prolate and oblate shaped ellipsoids and is be-

### page_13
H.J. Mattsson, S.A,. Elming : Precambrian Research 107 (2001) 265–281 277
lieved to be a result of both pure and simple shear
deformations. Rather narrow zones of N–S
trending planes of foliation cut this pattern. The
latter zones have sub-vertical magnetic lineation
and mainly prolate shaped anisotropy ellipsoids
and may therefore have undergone a dominant
pure shear deformation with dip-slip movement.
The N–S trending zones are younger than the
NNW–SSE pattern, but both fabrics appear to
follow the regional trend of the SEDZ and may
thus reﬂect two generations of deformation activ-
ity along the zone.
In the northern part of the SEDZ the magnetic
fabric of the deformed Revsund granite (sites
ST04–ST07) shows steeply dipping foliation and
a rotation of the lineation from sub-horizontal to
vertical when approaching the center of the SEDZ
(sites ST08–ST10, ST16 and ST21) (Fig. 4). The
pattern is consistent with pure-shear dominated
transpression (e.g. Tikoff and Teyssier, 1994;
Hrouda, 1994) probably caused by NNE–SSW
compressive deformation. Tikoff and Teyssier
(1994) show that the pure shear component devel-
ops faster than the simple shear component in this
environment, and the tectonic fabric will therefore
show a vertical lineation in highly deformed areas,
whereas it will show more of the strike-slip com-
ponent if the degree of deformation is lower. Our
data therefore support the conclusion made by
Bergman and Sjo¨stro¨m (1994) that the SEDZ is a
transpression zone developed in a NNE–SSW
compressive deformation. A change in the mag-
netic pattern is observed between the isotropic
fabric at sites ST01–ST03 and the anisotropic
fabric at sites ST04–ST07. This suggests that the
rock at sites ST04–ST07 was affected by the

at site ST23. The ellipse in (A) shows the 95% cone of conﬁdence of the mean. In (B) the plane of the dyke (great circle) and its

example of a thermal demagnetization from 150 to 600°C and the corresponding vector plot is shown. Open (closed) symbols in (D)
show vertical (horizontal) projection.

Fig. 11. The Apparent Polar Wander Path (APWP) for the
Fennoscandian Shield (after Elming et al., 1993). Closed sym-
bols along the APWP denote successive grand mean poles.
Symbols with a white cross denote paleopoles from this study,
shown with their circles of conﬁdence. (1) Dolerite sill forma-
tion mean direction (mean of sites ST16–ST20, Table 1). (2)
Dolerite dike (site ST23); the pole is calculated from the mean
remanence direction deﬁned from thermal demagnetization
data (Table 1). (3) The Ljusdal batholith (site KA02); the pole
is calculated from the mean remanence direction deﬁned from
AF demagnetization data (Table 1).
lineation, that is consistent at all ﬁve sites (ST11–
ST15, Fig. 4), and it may indicate a NW–SE
directed magma ﬂow (Bouillin et al., 1993). The
change in dip of the magnetic foliation planes
from sub-horizontal in the center to sub-vertical
at the edge probably shows how the magnetic
fabric is related to the shape of the pluton. The
magnetic fabric of this granite is therefore be-
lieved to display a magmatic ﬂow pattern of the
ﬁnal stages of the magma emplacement. It may
indicate that the Ra¨tan granite was emplaced in a
NW–SE directed extensive environment, which
contradicts a compressive environment as sug-
gested by Bergman and Sjo ¨stro¨m (1994). The
emplacement of the granite took place in an early
stage of the Gothian orogeny ( 1.75–1.55 Ga,
Gorbatschev and Bogdanova, 1993). The Gothian
orogeny and the magmatism of the TIB are sug-
gested to be related to subduction to the present
west of the Baltic Shield (Gaa ´l and Gorbatschev,
1987) and the TIB granites were emplaced in a
spreading environment (Ahl et al., 1999; A ,ha¨ll
and Larson, 2000), which is supported by our
data.
6.2. Ages of deformation
The 1.84 Ga old (U–Pb, Delin, 1993) Ljus-
dal batholith is thought to belong to a late stage
intrusion of subduction related magmatism during
the Svecofennian orogeny, occurring mainly in the
interval 1.9–1.86 Ga ago (A,ha¨ll and Larson, 2000
and references therein). The timing of the regional
metamorphism affecting the granodiorite is how-
ever still enigmatic. If the remanent magnetization
of the Ljusdal batholith (decl. 7° and incl. 
25°) is primary, a30° clockwise rotation and a
tilt of10° would be required in order to change
the direction from its expected direction (decl. 
335° and incl. 35°), corresponding to the 1.84
Ga reference pole on the APWP for the
Fennoscandian Shield (Fig. 11). A clockwise rota-
tion is not in accordance with the dextral shear of
the SEDZ and the dextral shear along the E–W
trending margin of the northern edge of the
batholith as suggested by Bergman and Sjo ¨stro¨m
(1994). A remagnetization therefore seems more
probable. Pressure and temperature estimates
SEDZ, whereas at sites ST01–ST03 the rock still
preserves a magmatic fabric. This change in fabric
may deﬁne the eastern boundary of this part of
the SEDZ, which then would be situated some-
where between the localities ST03 and ST04 (Fig.
4). The estimated width of the SEDZ based on
AMS data is here 20–25 km.
The 1.70 Ga old Ra ¨tan granite (U–Pb, Delin,
1996) has an average degree of magnetic an-
isotropy of P1.14, which is higher than many
sites inside the SEDZ. In the ﬁeld, however the
rock appears as almost isotropic and no micro-
scopic evidence indicates plastic deformation of
the granite. The relatively high P-value is most
likely related to the high mean susceptibility of
the rock (Fig. 7C). There is a sub-horizontal
NW–SE trending strike direction of the magnetic

### page_15
H.J. Mattsson, S.A,. Elming : Precambrian Research 107 (2001) 265–281 279
(Bergman and Sjo¨stro¨m, 1994) indicate that the
metamorphism affecting the Ljusdal batholith was
of amphibolite grade and therefore remagnetized
the rock. It is thus possible that the deﬁned
paleomagnetic age of 1.75–1.8 Ga is a meta-
morphic age and that there may be a causal
relation between the metamorphism and the em-
placement of the 1.80 Ga old (Claesson and
Lundqvist, 1995; Delin, 1996) Revsund granitoids.
If the remanence was acquired during or after the
metamorphism, the vector direction may have
been signiﬁcantly deﬂected from the direction of
the ambient ﬁeld at the time due to the high
degree of anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility
(P1.5). This degree of anisotropy could deﬂect
TRM by as much as 23° (Dunlop and
O8zdemir, 1997). Total deﬂection of the remanence
vector in a speciﬁc rock is difﬁcult to determine
unless one knows the ambient ﬁeld direction at
the time and place of magnetization, and also the
degree of anisotropy of the remanence carrier(s)
(e.g. Lowrie and Hirt, 1986; Cogne ´, 1988).
The undeformed Postjotnian sill that truncates
a plastic mylonite belonging to the SEDZ (site
ST16, Fig. 4), gives a minimum age of the plastic
deformation of the shear zone by 1250 Ma. It
also seems unlikely that the 1.5–1.6 Ga dolerite
dyke (site ST23), situated only 0.5–1 km east
of the zone center, would be unaltered if the zone
had been active after the intrusion of the dyke,
especially since the granodioritic host rock has a
NW–SE trending foliation parallel to the SEDZ.
The paleomagnetic data from this dyke therefore
indirectly show that the SEDZ is most likely older
than1.5–1.6 Ga.
The 1.80 Ga age of the SEDZ presented by
Ho¨gdahl et al. (1996) probably dates one defor-
mation event, but AMS and aeromagnetic data
indicate the possibility of multiple generations of
deformation. The development of a major shear
zone such as the SEDZ ( \200 km in length and
10–25 km wide) most likely occurred over a
period of millions of years. The age of the titan-
ites is approximately coeval with the 1.80 Ga
old Revsund granitoid (Claesson and Lundqvist,
1995) but the Revsund granite is deformed by the
SEDZ (this study) and this indicates deformation
along the SEDZ after 1.80 Ga ago. Early TIB-
magmatism (1.81–1.77 Ga) is believed to have
occurred in relation with eastward subduction
(Ahl et al., 1999; A ,ha¨ll and Larson, 2000), but
whether the tectonic conditions were governed by
extension (favored by A,ha¨ll and Larson, 2000) or
compression (favored by Ahl et al., 1999) is still
debated. The compressive deformation along the
SEDZ indicated in this study support Ahl et al.
(1999), however our data indicate compression
more from the present SSW than west. North-
ward compression at 1.80 Ga is reported in
southwestern Finland (Lindroos et al., 1996),
which together with our data indicate the possible
existence of a regional northward compressive
stress ﬁeld at that time. The timing of early TIB-
magmatism (1.81–1.77 Ga as indicated by A ,ha¨ll
and Larson, 2000; Ahl et al., 1999) and of the
SEDZ (1.80 Ga, Ho ¨gdahl et al., 1996; and
possibly younger, this study), suggests an overlap
of10 m.y. between northward compressive de-
formation and eastward subduction. To ﬁt the
early TIB-magmatism with a northward compres-
sion A,ha¨ll and Larson (2000) suggest a change in
the stress conditions at 1.81 Ga, which however is
10 m.y. to early according to the existing radio-
metric dating (Ho¨gdahl et al., 1996). The geologi-
cal evolution in the beginning of the Gothian
orogeny (1.75–1.70 Ga, Gaa ´l and Gorbatschev,
1987) is still enigmatic, and the period between
1.80 and 1.75 Ga ago may represent an initial
stage of this orogeny. It is therefore possible that
the compressive stress ﬁeld from the present SSW
indicated in this study is related to an initial stage
of plate collision. This collision between the
southwestern Scandinavian subprovince and older
parts of the Fennoscandian Shield resulted in a
system of regional NW–SE trending intra-plate
deformation zones, one of which is the SEDZ
(Fig. 12). At this time, or somewhat later, the
Fennoscandian Shield is also amalgamated to the
Ukrainian Shield (Elming et al., in press) possibly
forming a Pre-Rodinian supercontinent.
